3542:
The surviving text is Moses' farewell to Joshua before his death. Moses hands Joshua secret books and predicts Israel's history: the conquest, the division of the kingdom, the Babylonian exile, the return, wicked priests and kings, a powerful insolent king (clearly Herod the Great) who will rule 34 years, and his sons who will rule for shorter times. A persecution follows, during which a Levite named Taxo and his seven sons resolve to die rather than break the Law. Then God's kingdom appears, the devil is ended, and Israel is exalted to the stars. The manuscript breaks off as Joshua despairs and Moses reassures him.

Ancient writers mention an Assumption (or Ascension) of Moses that told of the archangel Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body. Origen and others said this was the source of Jude 9. Most scholars think the lost ending of our Testament of Moses, or a related work, contained that scene, though the exact relation between the Testament and the Assumption is debated.
3543: Moses' farewell prophecy to Joshua, retelling Israel's history up to Herod and the coming of God's kingdom. Ancient writers say a book like this told of the angel Michael and the devil arguing over Moses' body, which the letter of Jude mentions. It is not Scripture in any church.
3544: Moses commissions Joshua and gives him secret books (ch. 1)
3545: Prophecy of Israel's history: conquest, kingdoms, exile, return (ch. 2-4)
3546: Corrupt priests and an insolent king for 34 years (Herod) (ch. 5-6)
3547: Persecution and Taxo's resolve to die with his seven sons (ch. 8-9)
3548: Hymn of God's kingdom and the end of the devil (ch. 10)
3549: Joshua's grief and Moses' reassurance; text breaks off (ch. 11-12)
3550: No tradition ever listed it in its canon; it survived in a single damaged Latin copy. Its pseudonymous Mosaic frame, late date and loss in the original languages all kept it outside. The fact that Jude alludes to a tradition it contained was explained, as with Enoch, as Jude using a known story to make a point, not endorsing the whole book.
3551: Its main importance is for understanding Jude 9 and 2 Peter 2:11: Michael, not daring to bring a slanderous judgement against the devil, said, The Lord rebuke you. Scholars also value its view of history, its portrait of Herod's era from a pious Jewish perspective, and Taxo as a model of martyrdom expecting God to avenge.
3554: Conventional Jewish theology of covenant and judgement.
3555: Known to some Fathers, but never widely read.
3556: No liturgical or regular church use.
3558: Refers to the archangel Michael disputing with the devil about the body of Moses and saying The Lord rebuke you.
3559: Says Jude's account of Michael and the devil comes from a little book called the Ascension of Moses.
3560: Connects Jude 9 with the Assumption of Moses.
3562: Quotes passages from a Book of the Assumption of Moses.
3563: Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body; the tradition ancient writers traced to this work.
3564: Angels do not bring slanderous judgement, a likely echo of the same tradition.
3565: Moses dies and God buries him; no one knows his grave, the gap the tradition fills.
3566: Moses commissions Joshua, the setting for the Testament.
3567: The Lord rebuke you, Satan: the wording Michael uses in Jude.
3580: Greek original (only fragments survive); complete only in Ge'ez (Ethiopic), with Latin, Slavonic and Coptic parts.
3581: Christian prophetic circles of the late 1st or early 2nd century, probably in Syria or Palestine, possibly using an older Jewish story of Isaiah's martyrdom.
3582:
The first half (chapters 1-5) tells how King Manasseh, under the influence of the demon Beliar and a false prophet, has Isaiah sawn in two with a wooden saw; Isaiah dies steadfast, speaking with the Holy Spirit. Embedded in it is a Christian prophecy of the Beloved's coming, the apostles, the church's decline, and Beliar's appearance as a matricidal king (Nero).

The second half (chapters 6-11) is Isaiah's vision: an angel leads him up through the seven heavens to see God, the Beloved and the angel of the Holy Spirit worshipping. He then sees the Beloved descend secretly through the heavens, taking the form of each level's angels so as not to be recognised, be born of Mary in Bethlehem (with an unusual painless birth account), be crucified, descend to the dead, and rise and ascend in glory. It is one of the earliest Christian texts outside the New Testament on the hidden descent of Christ and the Trinity.
3583: A Christian work in two parts: the story of the prophet Isaiah being sawn in half by King Manasseh, and Isaiah's vision of travelling through seven heavens and seeing Christ come down secretly to be born, die and rise. It survives complete only in Ethiopic. It is not part of any official canon, though it is valued in Ethiopia.
3584: Manasseh turns to Beliar; Isaiah flees to the desert (ch. 1-2)
3585: Accusation and Christian prophecy of the Beloved and the church (ch. 3-4)
3586: Isaiah sawn in two with a wooden saw (ch. 5)
3587: Isaiah's ascent through the seven heavens (ch. 6-9)
3588: The Beloved's hidden descent, birth, crucifixion and ascension (ch. 10-11)
3589: Jews did not transmit it (though the rabbis knew a tradition that Manasseh killed Isaiah). Church writers grew suspicious of it: Jerome and Epiphanius report that it was used by heterodox groups (such as the Archontics and Hieracas), and its docetic-sounding descent of Christ in disguise and its distinctive angelology seemed unorthodox. It was therefore listed among apocrypha in the West and East.
3590: Ethiopian Christianity preserved it and values it as a revered writing (some lists of the broader Ethiopian canon include it; its formal status is debated). Scholars value it as early evidence for Christian prophecy, belief in the Trinity, the virgin birth, Christ's descent to the dead, and Nero-as-antichrist traditions. The Martyrdom story is the most likely source of the tradition that Hebrews 11:37 alludes to.
3592: Late 1st to early 2nd century, close to the apostolic age.
3593: Trinitarian and Christ-centred, but with a secret-descent Christology later judged suspect.
3595: Read in Ethiopia; used by some dissident groups elsewhere.
3597: Says the Jews sawed Isaiah in two with a wooden saw (a tradition the Martyrdom contains).
3598: Mentions an Ascension of Isaiah among apocryphal writings used by heretics.
3599: Reports that the Archontics and Hieracas used the Ascension of Isaiah.
3600: Some were sawn in two, usually taken to refer to the tradition of Isaiah's martyrdom.
3601: Manasseh shed much innocent blood in Jerusalem, the basis for the martyrdom story.
3602: Isaiah's vision of the Lord enthroned, expanded into a journey through seven heavens.
3603: Paul's ascent to the third heaven, another early Christian heavenly-journey account.
3604: The rulers of this age did not recognise the Lord of glory, close to the Ascension's hidden descent.
3611: Probably Hebrew original, translated into Greek and then Old Church Slavonic; survives only in Slavonic manuscripts (14th century and later), partly within the Palaea Interpretata.
3612: A Jewish author writing after the Temple's destruction in AD 70, probably in the land of Israel; some passages may be Christian or Bogomil additions.
3613:
The first part tells how young Abraham, working in the idol shop of his father Terah, realises the idols are powerless: one breaks, another burns, and he concludes that the true God must be the creator. God calls him, and his father's house is burnt with fire from heaven.

The second part expands the covenant sacrifice of Genesis 15. Guided by the angel Yahoel, who bears God's name, Abraham ascends on the wings of the sacrificial birds to the heavenly throne, sees the fiery chariot and the creation below, and is shown a picture of the world divided between Israel and the nations. The fallen angel Azazel, who tempted Adam and Eve, tries to deter him. Abraham sees the Temple destroyed and is told of a future judgement and of an elect one who will gather the people. Its throne-chariot vision is an early example of Jewish mystical traditions.
3614: A Jewish book from about AD 100 in which Abraham first sees through his father's idols, and then, guided by an angel, rises to heaven and sees God's throne, the history of the world and the Temple's destruction. It survives only in Old Slavonic. No church counts it as Scripture.
3616: God's call and the command to sacrifice (ch. 9-14)
3617: The angel Yahoel and Azazel the tempter (ch. 10-14)
3618: Ascent to the fiery throne and vision of creation (ch. 15-21)
3619: History, the destroyed Temple and the coming judgement (ch. 22-32)
3620: It was never proposed as Scripture in any community we know of. It vanished from Jewish and Greek-speaking Christian use and survived only through Slavonic Orthodox compilations of Bible history, where it served as an edifying story rather than canon.
3621: Scholars value it for early Jewish throne-mysticism, angelology (Yahoel bearing God's name, Azazel as Satan figure), and for Jewish reflection on the destruction of the Temple. It also preserves the popular story of Abraham rejecting idols, also found in Jubilees and later rabbinic midrash (Genesis Rabbah 38).
3624: Monotheistic and anti-idolatrous; some dualistic passages may be later additions.
3627: Presents itself as revelation to Abraham.
3629: A Slavonic Orthodox retelling of Old Testament history that incorporates the Apocalypse of Abraham.
3631: Reconstructed and studied its probable Greek and Hebrew background.
3632: The covenant sacrifice and Abraham's deep sleep, which the book turns into a heavenly ascent.
3633: Terah, Abraham's father, served other gods.
3634: Terah and Abraham leave Ur, the setting of the idol story.
3635: Ezekiel's fiery throne-chariot, the model for Abraham's vision.
3636: Stephen's summary of God's call to Abraham in Mesopotamia.
3648: Greek (Apocalypse of Moses) and Latin (Vita) are the main versions; also Armenian, Georgian and Slavonic. A Hebrew original has been proposed but is unproven.
3649: Disputed: either a Jewish work of the 1st century AD or a Christian composition from Jewish traditions; it circulated in many church communities in different forms.
3650:
This family of texts tells what happened to Adam and Eve after Eden. In the Latin version they repent by standing in rivers, Eve in the Tigris for 37 days and Adam in the Jordan for 40, but Satan, disguised as an angel of light, deceives Eve again. Satan explains his hostility: when Adam was created in God's image, Michael commanded the angels to worship him, and Satan refused and was cast out.

As Adam nears death, Eve and Seth travel to Paradise to ask for oil from the tree of mercy, but Michael tells them it will be given only at the end of time. Eve tells her children the story of the Fall. Adam dies, angels intercede, and God takes his soul to Paradise in the third heaven, promising resurrection. The tale shaped medieval legends such as the Holy Rood (wood from Eden's tree becoming the Cross) and has close parallels in the Qur'an's account of Iblis refusing to bow to Adam.
3651: Stories about Adam and Eve after leaving Eden: their repentance, Satan's second trick, why Satan fell (he refused to honour Adam), and Adam's death and promised resurrection. It exists in several languages and versions. It was never Scripture, but it influenced Christian art, legend and even the Qur'an.
3652: Adam and Eve hungry outside Paradise; penance in the rivers
3653: Satan deceives Eve again and tells the story of his fall
3654: Births of Cain, Abel and Seth; Cain's murder
3655: Eve's account of the Fall (Apocalypse of Moses 15-30)
3656: Seth and Eve seek the oil of mercy
3657: Adam's death, angelic intercession and burial in Paradise
3658: Never presented as a canonical book anywhere. It is a narrative expansion of Genesis with no claim to prophecy, of uncertain origin and existing in many differing versions. The so-called Gelasian Decree (6th century) lists a Penitence of Adam among apocrypha not to be received.
3659: It is a window into how Jews and Christians imagined the consequences of the Fall, the origin of Satan's enmity, repentance and the hope of resurrection. Its influence on medieval literature, art and legend (Seth's quest, the wood of the Cross) is large, and it sheds light on Paul's remark that Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
3661: Perhaps 1st century AD, though possibly much later.
3662: Teaches repentance and resurrection; Satan's fall story is speculative.
3663: Widely read but never received as Scripture.
3664: Popular in devotion and legend, not liturgy.
3665: The Greek version is framed as revealed to Moses; the Latin makes no claim.
3667: Lists a book called the Penitence of Adam among apocryphal works not received by the church.
3668: Gary A. Anderson and Michael E. Stone
3669: Published a synopsis of all the language versions side by side.
3670: The Fall and expulsion from Eden, which the book continues.
3671: The birth of Seth, who plays a major role in the story.
3672: Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, as he does when deceiving Eve again (Vita 9).
3673: Paradise in the third heaven, where God places Adam (Apocalypse of Moses 37).
3674: Let all God's angels worship him, applied to the Son; the book has angels commanded to honour Adam as God's image.
3685: An Alexandrian Jew writing as Aristeas, a Gentile courtier of Ptolemy II Philadelphus (285-246 BC), to his brother Philocrates.
3686:
This is the earliest account of how the Torah came to be translated into Greek, the beginning of the Septuagint. Aristeas says that Demetrius of Phalerum, the royal librarian, urged Ptolemy II to obtain the Jewish Law for the Alexandrian library. The king freed Jewish slaves, sent lavish gifts to Jerusalem, and the high priest Eleazar sent 72 elders, six from each tribe. After a week of banquets in which they answer the king's questions on government and virtue with wisdom, they translate the Law on the island of Pharos in 72 days. The Jewish community approves the translation and pronounces a curse on anyone who alters it.

Along the way Eleazar gives an allegorical defence of the food laws (clean animals teach justice and gentleness), and there is an idealised description of Jerusalem and the Temple. Historians doubt many details (Demetrius probably did not serve Ptolemy II), but agree the Torah was translated in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC. Later writers embellished the story so that the translators worked separately and produced identical texts, a miracle Jerome rejected.
3687: A story, told by a supposed Greek courtier, of how 72 Jewish scholars translated the Law of Moses into Greek for King Ptolemy's library in Alexandria. It is the origin of the name Septuagint (the Seventy). No one ever treated it as Scripture, but it shaped how Jews and Christians viewed the Greek Bible.
3688: The king's librarian proposes translating the Jewish Law
3689: Release of Jewish captives and gifts to Jerusalem
3690: Eleazar's defence of the food laws as moral symbols
3691: Description of Jerusalem, Temple and land
3692: Seven banquets of questions and wise answers
3693: Translation in 72 days and its approval by the Jewish community
3694: It was never proposed as Scripture by any community; it is a narrative about Scripture, not a book of Scripture. Its claim to be written by a Gentile eyewitness is regarded as a literary fiction.
3695: It explains the origin and authority of the Septuagint, the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of the New Testament writers. Philo and Josephus retold it, and Christian Fathers (Justin, Irenaeus, Augustine) used expanded versions to argue that the Greek Old Testament was divinely inspired. That belief became one of the main arguments for the wider (Septuagint-based) canon. Jerome, by contrast, dismissed the legend of separate cells and preferred the Hebrew.
3697: Defends the Law and the one God.
3699: No liturgical use; used as historical testimony.
3701: Paraphrases much of Aristeas' account of the translation.
3703: Tells of the translation and an annual festival on Pharos, calling the translators prophets.
3704: Tells the expanded story that the translators worked separately yet produced identical texts by God's inspiration.
3705: Rejects the legend of the seventy cells, saying the translators were interpreters, not prophets.
3706: The food laws Eleazar defends by allegory.
3707: The nations will call Israel wise because of its statutes, the attitude Aristeas dramatises.
3708: Do not add to or take away from the word, echoed in the curse on altering the translation.
3709: An example of the New Testament quoting the Old in its Greek (Septuagint) form (compare Deut 32:43 in Greek).
3723: The Yahad (community) associated with Qumran on the Dead Sea, widely identified with the Essenes; found in Cave 1 in 1947 with ten more copies in Cave 4.
3724:
The Community Rule is the founding charter of a Jewish sect that withdrew from the Jerusalem Temple, which it considered polluted, to live in strict purity by the Dead Sea. It describes the annual covenant ceremony with blessings and curses, the admission of members through stages of testing over two years, shared property, communal meals and study, and a penal code (for example, penalties for falling asleep in the assembly or speaking foolishly).

Its Treatise on the Two Spirits teaches that God created a spirit of truth and a spirit of falsehood, light and darkness, that struggle in every person until the final visitation. The community saw itself as a living temple whose prayer and obedience atone for the land, and it applied Isaiah 40:3 (prepare in the wilderness the way of the Lord) to its study of the Law, the same verse all four Gospels apply to John the Baptist. It expects a prophet and the messiahs of Aaron and Israel.
3725: The rule book of the Dead Sea Scrolls community, explaining how members joined, shared property, prayed and were disciplined, and teaching a struggle between light and darkness. It shows what a strict Jewish group near the time of Jesus believed. It was never meant to be Scripture for anyone outside that group.
3726: Purpose: to love the children of light and hate the children of darkness (col. 1)
3729: Rules for members, admission and shared property (cols. 5-7)
3730: The community as a holy house in the wilderness; Isaiah 40:3 (col. 8)
3731: Expectation of a prophet and the messiahs of Aaron and Israel; the hymn of the Master (cols. 9-11)
3732: It was never proposed as Scripture. It is a sectarian rule book for one community, and the movement that produced it disappeared after the Romans destroyed Qumran around AD 68. Its writers themselves treated it as rules for members, not as a prophetic book for all Israel. It is included here as an example of a text found among the scrolls that was never canonical.
3733: For historians and Bible readers it is invaluable: it shows a Jewish group contemporary with Jesus that practised baptism-like purifications, shared goods (compare the early church in Acts), used light-and-darkness language similar to John's Gospel, and expected a coming prophet and messiahs. It also helps explain why John the Baptist and Jesus were understood as they were, while making the differences (Jesus' meals with sinners, love for enemies) stand out sharply.
3734: A Jewish sectarian text; apostolicity does not apply.
3736: Jewish but sectarian: it rejects the Temple leadership and commands hatred of the sons of darkness.
3737: Used only by the Qumran community and its allies.
3738: Never read in synagogue or church.
3739: Presents itself as rules for the Master and members, not revelation.
3740: Describes Essene admission stages, shared property and discipline in terms strikingly like the Rule.
3742: Published the first edition of the Cave 1 scroll under the title Manual of Discipline.
3743: Prepare the way of the Lord in the wilderness, which the Rule (1QS 8.13-14) applies to the community's study of the Law.
3744: Matthew applies the same Isaiah verse to John the Baptist.
3745: John the Baptist identifies himself with the voice in the wilderness.
3746: The Jerusalem believers share possessions, a practice the Rule makes compulsory for full members.
3747: Become sons of light, language shared with the Rule's children of light.
3748: Love your enemies, a contrast with the Rule's command to hate the sons of darkness.
3756: War of the Sons of Light against the Sons of Darkness
3761: The Qumran community or related circles; found in Cave 1 in 1947 with further fragments in Cave 4.
3762:
The War Scroll is a detailed plan for the final war between the Sons of Light (Israel's faithful, especially the sect) and the Sons of Darkness (Belial's forces, the nations, and especially the Kittim, probably the Romans). The war will last forty years with sabbatical rests, in seven phases: three times the light will prevail, three times darkness, and in the seventh God's mighty hand will win.

Much of the scroll reads like a military manual with a priestly overlay: the sizes and inscriptions of banners and trumpets, the formations of the infantry and cavalry, the ages of soldiers, and the priests who sound the trumpets and pray. The archangel Michael leads the angelic army alongside Israel. It is a vivid example of how some Jews before Jesus expected the kingdom of God to come through holy war.
3763: A battle plan for the final war between good and evil, written by the Dead Sea Scrolls community, with banners, trumpets, priests and angels fighting alongside the faithful. It shows how some Jews expected God's kingdom to come by war. It was never Scripture for anyone.
3764: The war against the Kittim and the forty years (col. 1-2)
3765: Trumpets and banners with their inscriptions (col. 2-4)
3767: Priestly prayers and speeches before battle (col. 10-14)
3768: The final battle: Michael's rule and God's victory (col. 15-19)
3769: Never proposed as Scripture by any community; it is a sectarian programme for an expected war. Its tradition ended with the destruction of Qumran in the Roman war. It is listed here as an example of the many texts found in the Dead Sea caves that were valued by one group but never part of anyone's Bible.
3770: It shows the vocabulary of light and darkness, Belial, and Michael's war in heaven that also appears in the New Testament, and helps readers see what was different about Jesus' and the apostles' teaching: their war is not against flesh and blood, and the Lamb conquers by his death. It is also a major source for understanding Jewish expectations of the Roman threat.
3772: Jewish monotheism, but with a sectarian and militant eschatology.
3775: A rule for the war, not a claimed prophecy.
3777: Acquired and first published the Cave 1 War Scroll for the Hebrew University.
